conceptTag: Take the safe offer or keep your options?
readerTitle: The steady contract that could have sunk the painting company
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (주택 도장 업체와 부동산 관리 회사) · 모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용
insight: 안전한 제안의 안전함은 계약서가 아니라 그 계약이 사라져도 버틸 수 있는 선택지에서 나온다.
misconception: 오래 보장된 큰 계약은 위험을 줄여 준다. 고객 한 곳에 매출이 몰려도 계약 기간 동안은 안전하다.

sources.text: 모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 시뮬레이션
이 유닛의 개념 레슨 (THK-09-01 단기·장기 트레이드오프, THK-09-02 선택권, THK-09-04 시나리오 사고, THK-09-06 평판의 복리)

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 가상입니다. 비율 확인: 1차 결정 후 부동산 회사 40%, 주택 고객 60%. 2차 결정 후 50%. 5번 카드에서 계약이 절반으로 줄면 매출의 약 25%(50% × 1/2)가 사라지는 것으로 계산했습니다.
7번 카드의 '당장 급여를 못 줄 상황이면 안전한 제안을 먼저 받는다'는 THK-04-05(파산 위험) 개념과 연결됩니다. 특정 국가의 계약법이나 독점 조항 해석은 다루지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The steady contract that could have sunk the painting company
body: Dana runs a six-person house-painting crew. Most of her work comes from homeowners, and most homeowners come from referrals.
Then a property manager with 40 apartment buildings calls. They want her crew for three years. Steady work, guaranteed. You are Dana. Three decisions follow.

image.label: A painter holding a contract between a house and an apartment block
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 페인트가 묻은 작업복을 입은 여성 사장이 계약서를 들고 갈림길에 서 있다. 왼쪽엔 작은 주택들, 오른쪽엔 큰 아파트 단지. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Sign the three-year deal?
body: The offer: three years, first call on about 80% of your crew's time, at rates 15% below what homeowners pay. Payroll would be covered every month. What do you do?

options.text: Sign it. Three years of covered payroll is hard to turn down
options.feedback: You get certainty, but 80% of your revenue now depends on one client who can push the price. You'd also turn away homeowners, and referrals stop when you keep saying no.

options.text: Decline. Homeowners pay more and you stay independent
options.feedback: You keep your margins and freedom. You also give up steady work that would smooth out your slow winter months.

options.text: Counter: one year, renewable, up to 40% of crew time
options.feedback: You get a floor of steady work and keep your homeowner pipeline alive. The cost: they may say no, or offer less.

cards.title: Say you chose the counteroffer. Now they want more.
body: They agreed to one year at 40%. Six months in, they're happy. They offer to double your volume if you cut your rate another 10%. Filling the crew would feel great.

options.text: Accept. More volume keeps everyone busy
options.feedback: You'd be back near 80% reliance, at a thinner margin. One budget cut on their side would mean layoffs on yours.

options.text: First sketch three futures: they stay, they cut back, they leave. Take only what you could survive losing
options.feedback: The sketch shows you survive losing them at 40% or 50%, but not at 80%. You offer 50% at your current rate, and they accept.

options.text: Say no and keep the 40% cap
options.feedback: Safe, and your options stay open. But you skip checking whether some of the extra work could pay off.

cards.title: Say you chose to plan for three futures. Then a kitchen starts peeling.
body: A homeowner calls. The kitchen your crew painted last spring is peeling. Your crew used the wrong primer. A redo takes two crew-days, in a week booked for the property manager.

options.text: Offer a discount on their next job instead
options.feedback: You save two days now. But they live with a peeling kitchen, and their neighbors hear why.

options.text: Move two painters for two days, redo it free, and tell the property manager about the short delay
options.feedback: It costs about two days of revenue and one awkward call. The homeowner sends you three neighbors that summer.

options.text: Book the redo in three weeks, when the crew is free
options.feedback: Cheaper on your schedule, and the job gets fixed. But the customer waits, and the goodwill you earn back is smaller.

cards.title: The safe client didn't stay safe.
body: The property manager is sold. The new owners move maintenance to one large vendor and cut Dana's contract in half. She loses about a quarter of her revenue overnight.
It hurts, but it's the "they cut back" future she had sketched. Her homeowner work is still there, and so is a waiting list of referrals. Within weeks, most of the gap is filled.
Had she signed the three-year, 80% deal, a buyout clause or a price squeeze could have left her crew with almost nothing.

image.label: Revenue split before and after the client cut
image.brief: 두 개의 원형 차트 비교. 왼쪽 "Before": Property manager 50%, Homeowners 50%. 오른쪽 "After": Property manager 25%, Homeowners 75% (대기 명단에서 채워진 부분을 다른 색으로 표시). 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Safety comes from options, not promises.
body: A long contract feels safe because it promises the future. But promises can be bought out, renegotiated or cut. Real safety is having **somewhere else to go** when a promise breaks.
Each of Dana's best choices kept a door open: a shorter term, a cap she could survive losing, and a reputation that kept referrals coming.
cards.softwareNote: A startup gets the same offer when one enterprise customer wants a big custom deal. Signing can fund a year, but if that customer drives the roadmap, the product drifts away from everyone else. Caps on custom work and shorter terms keep your other options open.

cards.title: Options cost something.
body: Dana gave up guaranteed money. Keeping capacity free means some slow weeks, and a lower rate on a smaller deal.
If you can't make payroll next month, survival comes first. Take the safe offer, then rebuild your options from there. Keeping options open is a luxury of businesses that can already pay their bills.
And a safe offer isn't always a trap. A short term, an exit clause or a volume cap can give you both.

cards.title: Take the safe offer only in a size you could survive losing.
body: Each decision in Dana's year matches an idea from this unit:
list: **Decision 1, the counteroffer:** optionality. A shorter, smaller deal kept other doors open.
**Decision 2, the three futures:** scenario thinking. She sized the deal for the bad future, not the happy one.
**Decision 3, the free redo:** reputation compounds. Two lost days became years of referrals.
**The whole year:** short-term vs long-term. Each time, she gave up a little now to stay strong later.
cards.callout: **Try it today:** list your three biggest customers or contracts. For each one, write what would happen if it ended next month.
